title: Itô versus Stratonovich for shot noise with state-dependent amplitude: why the answer is Marcus
abstract: For Gaussian white noise the Itô and Stratonovich prescriptions differ by $O(dt)$ per time step, which accumulates into the familiar spurious drift $\tfrac12 D\,II'$. We show that for renewal shot noise with state-dependent gain, $\dot x=-C(x)-I(x)ξ[t]$ with $ξ[t]$ a train of Dirac spikes of finite random amplitude, the two prescriptions differ by a finite amount at every event, and that where $I$ vanishes the difference can become qualitative. The Marcus kick, the jump-process counterpart of the Stratonovich prescription, is the flow map of $dx/ds=I(x)$: no kick can cross a zero $x^\ast$ of $I$, for any jump and waiting-time statistics. The Itô kick is only the tangent map of that flow. For $I(x)=1+βx$ it crosses $x^\ast=-1/β$ if and only if $ξβ>1$ and collapses the whole line onto $x^\ast$ at $ξβ=1$; below threshold it is itself a Marcus kick with a remapped jump law. Bounded jump laws thus have a threshold, while unbounded ones leak across the barrier for \emph{any} parameters. The discrepancy cannot be absorbed into a renormalised drift beyond lowest order, and only the Marcus kick is generated by a single operator, which makes the master equation of Bianucci, Bologna and Mannella (2026) intrinsically Marcus. Numerically, the standard Heun kick is a second-order truncation of the Marcus map that preserves the barrier only because its order is even; it shortens every jump, biasing second moments in proportion to the squared jump amplitude and the jump kurtosis, and depleting the region near the barrier. We give the exact-flow integrator that replaces it.
summary: This paper resolves the ambiguity in applying stochastic calculus to systems driven by impulsive, state-dependent noise (shot noise). It rigorously demonstrates that the Marcus kick, derived from the underlying flow map, is the physically correct description, especially near barriers where the Itô interpretation fails. This has significant implications for accurately modeling transport phenomena in condensed matter and biophysics.
main_problem: The paper compares the mathematical validity of the Itô, Stratonovich, and Marcus interpretations for stochastic differential equations driven by non-Gaussian, state-dependent shot noise (Dirac spikes).
main_result: The Marcus kick, derived from the flow map of the underlying autonomous equation, is shown to be the physically correct description because it preserves the flow structure and correctly models barrier behavior, unlike the Itô kick.
method: The analysis involves comparing the resulting jump operators (kicks) derived from the three formalisms, particularly focusing on their behavior when the drift function $I(x)$ has zeros.
model_or_system: The model is a stochastic process driven by renewal shot noise, described by $\dot{x} = -C(x) - I(x)\xi[t]$, where $\xi[t]$ is a train of Dirac spikes with finite random amplitude.
key_observables: The difference between the three kicks, barrier crossing behavior at $I(x)=0$, and the structure of the resulting master equation operator.
important_parameters: The jump amplitude ($\xi_q$), the parameters defining the gain function $I(x)$, and the comparison between finite jumps versus continuous white noise.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the noise is composed of finite-amplitude Dirac spikes, making the difference between the formalisms a finite, non-perturbative effect, unlike the $O(dt)$ difference for Gaussian white noise.
figures_summary: Figures compare kink locations in probability distributions for different schemes (Itô, Marcus, Heun) at various jump amplitudes, and tables quantify the relative bias of $\langle x^2 angle$ between schemes.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing the physical model (shot noise), then comparing the mathematical formalisms (Itô vs. Marcus), demonstrating the topological differences (barrier vs. threshold), and finally comparing the exact Marcus kick against numerical approximations like the Heun kick.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical distinction between stochastic calculus interpretations for non-Gaussian noise is crucial for correctly modeling physical systems like synaptic plasticity or charge transport where noise is impulsive, providing a necessary correction beyond standard Itô/Stratonovich treatments.
